item.title: Two Straits, One Chokehold: How the Houthis Took Control of the Bab el-Mandeb Shipping Lane
item.body:
## A Week That Redrew the Red Sea's Map

In the span of little more than a week, Iran-aligned Houthi forces have completed a rapid military campaign that leaves them in effective control of the Yemeni side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow waterway that funnels shipping between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, and onward to the Suez Canal.

The offensive began on September 3 with a push to sever the road linking the city of Taiz to the port of Mokha. Within days, Houthi units had taken Mokha, the town of Dhubab, and the strategically placed island of Mayyun near the strait's mouth. Government forces then withdrew from Perim Island, the outpost that splits Bab el-Mandeb into its two navigable channels, handing the Houthis command of both passages. The group went on to seize the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands further north, rounding out its hold on the strait's key waypoints.

## Why the Strait Matters

Bab el-Mandeb is one of the world's most consequential maritime chokepoints, carrying a significant share of the traffic that would otherwise transit the Suez Canal, including a large volume of Gulf oil exports bound for Europe and beyond. Control of the strait's Yemeni shoreline gives the Houthis — and by extension their backers in Tehran — leverage over shipping lanes that Red Sea nations and global carriers depend on.

Analysts have noted the timing is especially pointed: the gains come as Iran maintains pressure on the Strait of Hormuz, the passage on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula through which a large share of the world's seaborne oil moves. Together, the two chokepoints give Iran-aligned forces influence over maritime routes on both flanks of the peninsula, a development that has unsettled energy markets and regional governments alike.

## Houthi Assurances, Regional Unease

A senior Houthi politburo official sought to reassure international shipping firms and regional governments, saying the group poses "no danger" to Red Sea cargo traffic and that "freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly." Neighboring states and shipping insurers have so far treated those assurances cautiously, watching for any disruption to transit through the corridor.

Houthi fighters are now reported to be positioned close to the African side of the strait, a reminder of how tightly the group now grips the chokepoint's approaches.

## The Human Cost

The campaign has come at a heavy price for Yemeni civilians. Aid officials say the week of fighting has left several hundred people dead and forced tens of thousands from their homes, with the UN's migration agency estimating roughly 46,000 people displaced by the violence. Humanitarian groups are appealing for access to affected coastal communities as the front lines shift.

## What Comes Next

For now, shipping and energy markets are watching closely rather than reacting sharply, as vessel movements through Bab el-Mandeb continue despite the change in territorial control. But the durability of the Houthis' assurances, the response from Gulf states and Western navies, and the broader trajectory of the wider regional conflict will likely determine whether this becomes a lasting shift in who holds leverage over one of the planet's busiest trade arteries — or the opening chapter of a longer struggle for the Red Sea's southern gate.
